claim: Do not treat 60-30-10 as a target ratio for product interfaces; treat it only as a starting heuristic for compositions where all three colours carry visual weight.
why: The example given shows a well-regarded product shipping a roughly 90/8/2 split, which means the conventional ratio is not what strong product UI actually does — the rule is a general-purpose composition aid, not a product-UI spec.
when: Building application or dashboard interfaces where a neutral surface hosts dense content and controls.
fails: Marketing pages, brand collateral, or illustration work, where the balanced three-part split still reads well because there is no dense functional content competing for attention.

claim: Let the dominant neutral occupy roughly 90% of the surface, a secondary neutral around 8%, and reserve the accent for 2% or less — and accept screens where the accent never appears.
why: Product screens are mostly chrome and content; colour that is spent on decoration competes with colour that is spent on signalling. Starving the accent is what makes it legible as a signal when it does appear.
when: Laying out product screens with a fixed neutral base and one action/brand colour.
fails: Interfaces whose primary job is expressive or categorical — data visualisation, media browsers, colour-coded workflows — where multiple saturated hues are the content itself.

claim: Treat 'no accent colour on this screen' as a valid outcome rather than a gap to fill.
why: If the accent's job is to mark the one thing that matters, a screen with nothing to mark should not have one; forcing it in trains users to ignore it.
when: Reviewing a screen that has no primary action, no error state, and no destination the user must be pushed toward.

claim: For a product UI, budget four background levels, one to two stroke values, and three text values as the minimum neutral set — then add chart colours and hover/active states on top of that count.
why: A dashboard nests surfaces inside surfaces (frame, canvas, card, nested card) and needs separation at each depth; a palette scoped to a landing page runs out of steps and forces you to reuse a value where you need contrast.
when: Defining neutral tokens for an app, dashboard, or any interface with nested containers.
fails: Marketing and landing pages, where three to five neutrals total is sufficient and a larger set adds unused tokens.

claim: Do not set the app canvas to pure white; reserve pure white for the surfaces that must sit on top, such as cards.
why: If the background is already the lightest possible value, you have no headroom to make a card read as raised — cards can only go darker or rely on shadow, which removes a whole arrangement from the table.
when: Light-mode product interfaces where cards or panels sit on a page background.
fails: Layouts where cards are intentionally darker than the canvas (Notion-style), where a pure-white background is a deliberate choice.

claim: Make the persistent app frame — sidebar, top bar — only about 2% darker than the canvas rather than a strong grey.
why: Perceived contrast scales with area, so a large region needs far less lightness difference than a small one to read as a distinct zone; pushing it further makes the chrome compete with content.
when: Anchoring navigation chrome against a content area in light mode.
fails: Small elements, or dark mode, where a 2% step is too subtle to register.

claim: Define card edges with a light grey stroke around 85% white instead of a thin black or near-black border.
why: A dark hairline carries more visual weight than the content it contains and reads as a hard cut; a light stroke describes the boundary without becoming the loudest element on the surface.
when: Separating a card or panel from a background of similar lightness.
fails: High-contrast or accessibility-driven treatments where the boundary itself must meet a contrast threshold.

claim: When a card reads washed out against its background, fix it with a lightness step between the two surfaces rather than by adding a drop shadow.
why: Shadow is a weak separator on low-contrast pairings — it softens the problem without solving it, because the eye is reading surface lightness, not depth.
when: A card and its background sit too close in value.

claim: Pick one of three light-mode surface arrangements and hold it consistently: darker canvas with lighter cards, lighter canvas with darker cards, or evenly stepped monochromatic layers.
why: All three read correctly, but mixing them within one product makes elevation ambiguous — the user can no longer tell depth from lightness.
when: Establishing the surface system for a light-mode product.

claim: Reuse the frame/sidebar value as the darker-card value when the design calls for cards darker than the canvas.
why: Reusing an existing step keeps the neutral ramp tight and makes chrome and containers read as the same material.
when: Light background with darker cards.

claim: Encode button priority as darkness: ghost buttons at the light end, near-black with white text for the single primary action, and everything else between — with general-purpose buttons landing around 90–95% white.
why: A monotonic darkness scale gives an unambiguous, colour-independent ranking of actions, so the eye finds the primary action without relying on hue.
when: Setting up neutral button variants in a light-mode interface.

claim: Build text hierarchy from three steps: headings around 11% white, body around 15–20%, and secondary or supporting text at 30–40%.
why: Three well-separated values cover the full hierarchy while keeping body text short of pure black, which reduces harshness against a light surface.
when: Assigning neutral text colours in a light-mode product UI.
fails: Where the 30–40% subtext step drops below the contrast minimum for its size — small subtext may need to move darker.

claim: Express neutral tokens as a percentage of white and reason about them as positions on one ramp, rather than picking greys individually.
why: A single measurable scale lets you compare, space, and audit every neutral against the others, so decisions become arithmetic instead of eyeballing.
when: Defining or auditing a neutral palette.

claim: Define your brand colour as a tonal ramp (roughly 50 through 900) before using it anywhere, and reference steps by number rather than storing a single hex.
why: Every interactive state and every theme needs a different lightness of the same hue; a single value forces ad-hoc darkening at each use site and drifts out of sync.
when: Any time a product adopts an accent or brand colour that will appear in more than one component or state.

claim: In light mode, use the 500 or 600 step as the default accent, step to 700 on hover, and use 400-500 for inline links.
why: State changes need to be perceptible without changing hue, and a fixed step interval makes the change consistent everywhere.
when: Assigning interactive states to buttons, links, and other accent-coloured controls on a light background.

claim: Treat a neutral, accent-free palette as a legitimate choice rather than an unfinished one.
why: Some products build their identity on restraint; an accent is a functional tool, not an obligation.
when: Developer tools, infrastructure, and other products where the interface should recede behind content.
fails: When the product needs a memorable identity or has to differentiate in a crowded category — there, owning a hue does real work.

claim: Do not produce dark mode by inverting or mirroring the light palette; derive it separately from the same ramp.
why: A mirrored palette carries the light-mode step sizes with it, and those steps are too small to survive at the dark end of the scale.
when: Adding a dark theme to an existing light-mode design system.

claim: Roughly double the lightness gap between adjacent surfaces in dark mode: if light-mode surfaces sit about 2% apart, space dark-mode surfaces 4-6% apart.
why: Perceived contrast compresses at low luminance, so identical numeric steps read as a smaller difference — the separation has to be paid for in larger increments.
when: Setting background, card, and panel values for a dark theme.

claim: Shift the accent lighter for dark mode — use the 300 or 400 step as the base and 400 or 500 for hover.
why: A mid-ramp accent tuned for white backgrounds loses contrast against dark surfaces; moving up the ramp restores it without changing the hue you own.
when: Porting accent-coloured buttons, links, and highlights into a dark theme.

claim: In dark mode, dim text away from pure white and brighten borders relative to their light-mode counterparts.
why: Full-strength white text on a dark field glares over long sessions, while borders that were adequate on white effectively vanish on dark.
when: Tuning text and divider tokens for a dark theme, especially in tools people keep open all day.

claim: In dark mode, make surfaces lighter as they rise in elevation, with no exceptions; a card that cannot go lighter gets a border instead.
why: Dark mode has no shadow to signal depth — a shadow on a dark background is invisible — so lightness becomes the only available depth cue and must stay monotonic.
when: Layering modals, cards, popovers, and raised bars over a dark base.
fails: Light mode, where shadow carries elevation and a raised surface can stay the same value as its parent or go slightly darker.

claim: Give inset or flush controls like search bars a border rather than a lighter fill so they read as recessed, not raised.
why: Reserving lightness for genuine elevation keeps the depth signal unambiguous; a border delimits without implying the element sits above the surface.
when: Dark-mode form fields and controls that sit level with their container.

claim: Generate ramps with a palette tool rather than hand-picking steps, and generate them once so light and dark themes both draw from the same source.
why: Tool-generated ramps hold perceptual spacing consistent across the scale, and a shared source means the dark theme is a re-selection rather than a second palette to maintain.
when: Standing up the colour tokens for a new design system.

claim: Treat semantic colour (success, warning, error, in-progress) as a separate layer that is allowed to break your brand palette rather than be derived from it.
why: Semantic colour's job is instant comprehension, not brand expression; forcing it through brand hues destroys the meaning it is supposed to carry.
when: Any product surface with states, outcomes, or feedback — deploy logs, form validation, notifications, order status.
fails: Decorative or purely identity-driven surfaces (marketing hero, empty-state illustration) where no state is being reported; adding semantic colour there just adds noise.

claim: Render destructive actions in red even when red is nowhere in the brand palette.
why: Red is a near-universal learned signal for irreversible or dangerous action; overriding it with a brand hue removes the user's last warning before data loss.
when: Delete, revoke, cancel-subscription, and other irreversible controls in any product.
fails: Contexts where red already means something else in the domain (finance charts where red is a downward value, or locales where red reads as auspicious) — there the destructive signal needs a second cue such as an icon or confirmation step.

claim: A brand can be entirely monochrome and still communicate state, provided the semantic layer is added on top of it.
why: The neutral brand carries identity; the small semantic accents carry information, so the two roles do not compete.
when: Minimal or black-and-white brand systems that still need to report success, failure, and progress.

claim: Do not build data visualisations from neutrals only, and do not build them from tints of a single brand hue only.
why: An all-neutral chart gives the eye nothing to separate series by; a single-hue ramp makes adjacent series read as the same thing, so category distinctions collapse.
when: Multi-series charts — lines, stacked bars, pie or donut segments, categorical legends.
fails: Single-series or magnitude-only charts, where a one-hue sequential ramp is exactly the correct encoding.

claim: Build categorical chart palettes in OKLCH by fixing lightness and chroma once, then stepping hue by roughly 25–30 degrees per swatch.
why: OKLCH models human perception, so holding L and C constant makes every hue read at the same visual weight; stepping hue by a consistent interval keeps series distinct without any one dominating.
when: Generating a categorical spectrum of roughly 4–12 series colours for charts and data displays.
fails: When the extracted hues must also pass contrast requirements against the chart background or against each other for colour-blind users — the fixed L that looks even may still fail those checks and needs adjustment or a non-colour redundant encoding.

claim: Do not equate numerically equal colour values with equally prominent colours; pure green will out-shout pure blue at the same nominal brightness.
why: Human sensitivity to lightness varies by hue, so HSL or hex-level 'equal' values produce a palette where some series visually leap forward and skew what the reader thinks is important.
when: Any time you hand-pick or programmatically generate a multi-hue palette.

claim: Order your colour system so identity comes first and meaning is applied last, overriding identity where the two conflict.
why: A palette built purely for consistency will suppress the signals users depend on; treating meaning as the final, higher-priority layer resolves that conflict predictably.
when: Defining tokens for a design system that must serve both branding and functional communication.

claim: To create a themed (tinted) neutral ramp, don't hand-pick the tinted greys — take each existing neutral, convert it to OKLCH, subtract a small fixed amount of lightness (~0.03) and add a small fixed amount of chroma (~0.02), then set the hue to your theme hue.
why: Applying one uniform transform across every step preserves the relative contrast relationships the original ramp already encodes, so the themed ramp inherits the ramp's tested legibility instead of requiring it to be re-tuned by eye.
when: You have a working neutral scale and need a branded or themed variant of the same UI in one or many hues.
fails: Not addressed in the chapter; note that the transform is defined on neutrals only — reapplying it to already-saturated brand colors, or stacking it repeatedly, will drift lightness and oversaturate.

claim: Do the theming math in OKLCH rather than in hex, HSL, or RGB.
why: OKLCH separates lightness, chroma, and hue as independently editable channels that track human perception, so changing hue alone leaves perceived brightness intact — the same edit in HSL or RGB would shift apparent contrast unpredictably between hues.
when: Any programmatic color transform where you need the result to stay perceptually consistent across different hues.

claim: Keep hue as the only parameter that varies between themes; hold the lightness and chroma deltas constant across all of them.
why: One free variable means every theme is generated by the same function, so red, green, and blue variants are guaranteed to be siblings rather than three separately tuned palettes that drift apart.
when: Building multi-theme or multi-brand systems from one base design.
fails: Chroma at a fixed value reads differently per hue — yellows and greens hit gamut and appear more saturated than blues at identical chroma, so extreme hues may need a manual chroma trim.

claim: Add chroma to neutrals in small amounts (around 0.02 in OKLCH) — enough to tint, not enough to read as a color.
why: A tinted neutral should still function as a background or surface; large chroma turns it into a foreground color and destroys the neutral's job in the hierarchy.
when: Tinting surfaces, borders, and background greys toward a brand hue.

claim: Reach for the tint-the-neutrals technique first when building dark mode, not just for branded themes.
why: Pure grey dark surfaces read as flat and cheap; a small consistent chroma shift across the dark ramp gives depth, and the effect is more visible against dark backgrounds than light ones.
when: Producing a dark variant of an existing light design.

claim: Store the ramp as design tokens/variables so a theme swap is a change to the hue value rather than a re-edit of every layer.
why: The transform is only cheap if colors are referenced indirectly; hard-coded hex values force you to repeat the work per component.
when: Any design intended to ship more than one theme.

claim: Do not select colours by dragging into the top-right region of a square hex/HSB picker; move down and left to sample mid-saturation and mid-lightness values as first-class choices.
why: The top-right corner of the picker is the physically easiest place to land and produces maximally saturated, maximally bright hues, so an unexamined picker habit collapses a two-dimensional space into one point.
when: Choosing brand, accent, or surface colours by eye in any HSB-style colour field.
fails: A brief genuinely calls for high-energy saturation — sports, children's products, neon or arcade aesthetics — where a muted palette would read as timid.

claim: Treat a generated palette as a sampling tool, not a specification: take one or two hues that stand out and build the rest of the scheme around them rather than shipping all the suggested swatches.
why: Generators optimise for variety within a preview grid, not for the hierarchy of a specific interface; adopting the full set imports colours the design has no job for.
when: Using an online colour picker or palette generator to break out of a stale colour habit.
fails: The generator output is a tuned, tested system palette (an existing design system's ramp), where cherry-picking breaks internal contrast relationships.

claim: When picker-generated colours feel generic, sample hues from photographs, natural scenes, and existing artwork instead of inventing them numerically.
why: Unusual colours are hard to reach by abstract navigation of a picker, but they already exist in observed sources, so sampling shortcuts the search.
when: Hunting for a distinctive accent or brand hue that a generator has not surfaced.

claim: Use a deliberately narrow palette — a neutral, a grey, and one accent — while learning, then treat that constraint as a training wheel to be removed rather than a permanent style.
why: The restriction removes decisions while fundamentals are being built, but left unexamined it hardens into a habit that caps the range of work produced.
when: Early practice, or any period where colour decisions are consuming attention needed elsewhere.
fails: Later work where the same three-colour formula is applied reflexively to every brief regardless of tone or subject.

claim: Schedule periodic colour exploration as its own activity, separate from any live project, and record hues you find so they are available later.
why: Interesting colours are described as elusive and easy to overlook even though the whole gamut is technically available, which implies they surface through search rather than on demand mid-project.
when: Maintaining a personal palette library or refreshing a visual vocabulary between projects.

claim: Default to no gradient; add one only when it carries a specific job, and reach for a flat fill first.
why: Gradients are usually applied as decoration rather than to communicate anything, so removing them removes noise without removing meaning.
when: Backgrounds, cards, buttons, and surfaces where a designer is reaching for a gradient by habit.
fails: Cases where the gradient is doing real work — brand identity, depth cueing on a hero, or a scrim that keeps text legible over imagery.

claim: If a gradient is necessary, build it from two stops of the same hue at different lightness, not from two different hues.
why: Cross-hue blends pass through muddy intermediate colours and read as arbitrary; a single-hue ramp stays coherent and looks intentional.
when: Any decorative fill where a gradient survives the 'do I need this' test.
fails: Deliberate multi-hue brand gradients built by a designer who controls the interpolation space and midpoint colour.

claim: Never ship a tool's stock drop shadow — treat the default as a starting placeholder that must be edited before use.
why: Default shadows are tuned to be visible in a picker, not to match a real light source, so they read as heavy and instantly signal an untouched file.
when: Any elevation applied in Figma, Sketch, or a CSS framework's default shadow token.

claim: Soften a shadow by changing its colour to a light grey and raising the blur radius, rather than by lowering the opacity of the harsh black default.
why: Reducing opacity keeps the same hard falloff and just makes it fainter; changing the colour and spreading the blur changes the shape of the shadow so it reads as ambient light instead of a dark outline.
when: Any card, modal, dropdown, or button that needs a sense of elevation.
fails: Dark-mode surfaces, where a light-grey shadow becomes invisible or glows — there, elevation usually comes from raising the surface's own lightness instead.

claim: When an effect is under review, test removal before you test adjustment — if the layout still communicates hierarchy without it, leave it off.
why: Every effect adds visual noise, and less noise generally produces a stronger design, so the burden of proof sits on keeping the effect.
when: Auditing an existing design that feels cluttered or amateur.
fails: When the effect was the only thing separating two adjacent surfaces — removing it then collapses hierarchy and you need a border or spacing change to replace it.

claim: Distinguish elevation from decoration: use one restrained shadow style to express layering, and avoid stacking glows, gradients, and shadows on the same element.
why: Effects compete for attention; when several are combined on one component none of them reads as a deliberate signal.
when: Components where a designer is layering multiple effects to make something feel 'polished'.

claim: Budget your interface colour by area, roughly 60% dominant/neutral surface, 30% secondary, 10% accent — and check the actual proportions on the rendered screen, not just in the palette swatches.
why: A proportional split guarantees one colour reads as ground, one as structure, and one as the thing that earns the eye; without it every hue competes and none wins.
when: Composing or auditing any full screen or marketing section with more than one brand colour in play.
fails: Treated as a swatch-count rule rather than an area rule — the 60% can itself be a vivid brand colour and the 10% accent can be plain white, so the ratio describes coverage and dominance, not saturation.

claim: Cap the number of distinct accent colours in a single repeating component group at one; if a card row uses five different fills, that is a defect, not variety.
why: Accent colour is an attention signal, and issuing five signals simultaneously means the user gets no signal at all — the items read as equally urgent, which is the same as none being urgent.
when: Any set of sibling elements — cards, tiles, badges, list rows — rendered at the same hierarchy level.
fails: The colour is genuinely encoding a category or status the user must distinguish, in which case the hues are data, not decoration.

claim: Run every coloured surface and its text through a WCAG contrast check before accepting the combination; a colour pairing that fails the ratio is disqualified regardless of how it looks.
why: Contrast failure makes content unreadable for a real slice of users, which converts an aesthetic choice into a functional bug.
when: Any time text, icons, or meaningful marks sit on a coloured fill.

claim: Match a colour's visual weight to the element's importance in the hierarchy — do not spend your loudest, most saturated colour on a low-priority component.
why: Saturation is read as emphasis; a bright fill on a minor element inverts the page's hierarchy and pulls the eye away from what actually matters.
when: Deciding fill treatment for supporting components — secondary cards, ancillary panels, decorative containers.
fails: The element is the primary call to action or the intended focal point, where maximum weight is correct.

claim: When a brand colour is too heavy for its slot, lighten or desaturate it into a tint and switch the text to near-black rather than abandoning the colour.
why: A tint preserves brand identity and grouping while dropping the attention weight, and dark text on a light tint clears contrast requirements that white-on-saturated typically fails.
when: You want brand presence on a component that should not dominate the page.

claim: Render icons in the surrounding text or neutral colour by default; reserve coloured icons for cases where the colour communicates state — active, selected, error, success.
why: An icon's job is silhouette recognition, which colour does not improve; once colour is meaningless on most icons, it stops being readable as meaning on the ones that need it.
when: Icon sets in navigation, tab bars, feature lists, and inline UI affordances.
fails: Brand or illustrative iconography where colour is part of the identity, or multi-colour icons used as product/category marks.

claim: Audit each coloured element by asking what the colour communicates; if the only answer is 'it looked plain otherwise', return it to neutral.
why: Colour applied without a message adds noise that competes with colour applied with one, and removing it costs nothing while raising clarity.
when: Final polish pass over a design that feels busy or fatiguing.

claim: Test a colour decision by fixing the first problem and immediately re-evaluating for the problem the fix introduced, rather than shipping the first improvement.
why: Colour changes propagate through hierarchy and accessibility at once — unifying five accents into one solved the competition but created a dominance and contrast failure that only a second pass caught.
when: Any structural palette change on an existing screen.

claim: Default to a neutral grey page background with a lighter, near-white foreground for content surfaces; reserve saturated colour for elements that need attention.
why: A background exists to sit behind content. Any saturation there competes with the content in front of it and flattens the perceived hierarchy.
when: Standard light-mode product UI — dashboards, content apps, marketing surfaces with real content on them.
fails: Deliberately expressive contexts — landing heroes, brand splash screens, marketing moments — where the background is the content and there is little competing UI on top.

claim: In dark mode, invert the same value ordering rather than the concept: the darkest value is the page background and each surface that sits closer to the user gets a slightly lighter value.
why: Elevation is read as a value step away from the background in both modes, so the rule is about relative distance from the base layer, not about light versus dark.
when: Building a dark theme, or building light and dark themes as one token system.

claim: To get brand colour into surfaces without breaking neutral balance, mix a small amount of the brand hue into the neutral instead of using the brand colour at full saturation.
why: A tinted neutral reads as a coloured surface at a glance while keeping its value and chroma low enough that content on top still dominates.
when: Cards, panels, section backgrounds, and empty states that feel sterile in pure grey and need brand presence.
fails: When the tint is pushed far enough to become a real colour — at that point it competes with content and stops functioning as a background.

claim: You can reverse the light-mode default and put white on the smaller element over a slightly darker page, when the element is a small interactive control such as a search field or input.
why: For a small control, the brighter fill is what separates it from the page and marks it as interactive, and the contrast it gains helps legibility rather than hurting it.
when: Small, discrete UI components — search bars, inputs, chips, floating controls — inside a light layout.
fails: Large surfaces; inverting a full-page-width panel makes it read as the background again and loses the separation.

claim: When a nested surface would add a third or fourth value layer to a screen, delete the fill and define the element with a 1px border instead.
why: Every additional filled layer is another value the eye has to resolve; a border achieves the same grouping and boundary at almost no visual cost.
when: Cards inside already-tinted containers, or any element nested two or more surface levels deep.

claim: Treat colour distribution as the same job whitespace does — use large areas of low-chroma neutral to create separation, and spend saturation only where you want the eye to land.
why: Both whitespace and neutral area work by subtraction: they earn attention for the few elements that break the pattern.
when: Any screen where everything is competing for attention and the hierarchy has collapsed.

claim: Keep the number of distinct surface values on a screen small — background, foreground, and at most one nested level — and use borders past that point.
why: The chapter reaches for a border precisely at the point where a third layer would be needed, implying the layer budget runs out fast.
when: Layouts with nested containers — cards in sections in page shells.

claim: When a component needs several distinct colour values but the brand supplies only one, generate siblings by rotating that hue a short distance in both directions on the colour wheel rather than by stepping the same hue down in opacity.
why: Opacity steps only change how much of the same colour you see, so adjacent segments read as one washed-out mass; shifting hue gives each segment its own identity while staying visibly related to the brand.
when: Multi-part UI elements — segmented storage bars, stacked charts, category tags, status groups — built on a single-colour brand palette.
fails: When the segments are meant to express one quantity at different intensities (a heat scale, a progress fill), where a single hue with varying lightness communicates order better than separate hues.

claim: Pair the analogous set with one colour taken from the opposite side of the wheel and reserve it for the element that must stand out.
why: Analogous hues cohere but stay low-contrast against each other; a complement supplies the separation that makes one item read as the focal point.
when: A palette that already feels unified but lacks an accent for the primary action, the highlighted data series, or the alert state.
fails: If the complement is used at the same frequency and area as the base hues, it stops functioning as an accent and the palette reads as two competing brands.

claim: Keep every derived colour inside a nameable relationship to the brand hue — analogous neighbours or the direct complement — instead of picking additions by eye.
why: A palette assembled from defined wheel relationships looks deliberate and stays recognisably on-brand; arbitrary additions read as inconsistency.
when: Expanding any constrained brand palette for product UI.
fails: Domains with fixed colour conventions (green for success, red for destructive) where semantic meaning outranks wheel geometry.

claim: If a brand colour fails contrast against the text colour it must carry, darken the hue until it passes rather than shipping the failing pair or switching the text colour.
why: Darkening changes only lightness, so the colour stays identifiably the brand's while the text becomes legible; a failing pair is not a stylistic choice, it is a defect.
when: Saturated mid-tone brand colours — oranges, yellows, limes — used as button or badge backgrounds under white text.
fails: Where the brand colour must appear at its exact specified value (logo lockups, print-matched packaging), in which case pair it with dark text or move it out of the text-bearing role.

claim: Treat the complementary accent as a second escape hatch for contrast failures: if the brand hue cannot be darkened acceptably, use the passing complement for the text-bearing surface.
why: It solves legibility and palette expansion with the same move, so the fix does not introduce a colour that is otherwise unjustified in the system.
when: Primary buttons or filled chips whose brand-coloured version cannot reach the required contrast ratio without losing brand recognition.
fails: When the brand colour is the sole recognition cue for that control and users navigate by colour.

claim: Read brand guidelines as the starting point of a palette, not its full extent — extending them to meet legibility and hierarchy needs is part of the job, not a violation of them.
why: Guidelines are usually written for marketing surfaces and rarely anticipate the number of simultaneous colour roles a product UI requires; mature brands ship secondary and deepened variants for exactly this reason.
when: Any product work where the supplied palette cannot cover the interface's structural needs.
fails: Under strict brand governance or regulated identity systems, where the extension must be proposed and approved rather than assumed.

claim: Structure the extended palette as one dominant brand colour plus a deliberately chosen partner — either a contrasting hue or a deeper version of the same hue — rather than a flat set of equal colours.
why: Established brands use this primary-plus-secondary shape, which keeps ownership of the brand hue while giving the interface a second colour to work with.
when: Defining the top level of a product colour system before deriving tints and states.
fails: Interfaces that need many mutually distinguishable categorical colours, where a two-colour spine is not enough.

claim: Validate each derived colour against contrast requirements at the moment you pick it, not after the screens are built.
why: Colour choices made purely on the wheel can land in ranges that never pass with the intended text colour; checking during selection avoids rebuilding components later.
when: Any colour destined to sit behind text or interactive labels.

claim: Assign text colour by rank: primary content gets the darkest value, secondary metadata (file size, type, timestamps, helper text) steps down to a mid-dark gray, and tertiary labels step down again.
why: Colour value is a hierarchy channel; if every string is the same pure black, the interface flattens and the reader has to work out importance from position alone.
when: Any surface stacking content of unequal importance — list rows, cards, form fields, detail panes.
fails: Downgrading past the contrast floor: secondary text still has to clear WCAG AA (4.5:1 for body copy), so 'less important' cannot mean unreadable.

claim: Default body and heading text to a very dark gray or a near-black tinted with the brand hue rather than #000000.
why: A pure-black-on-white edge is harsher than the rest of the palette and reads as untuned; a tinted dark carries the product's colour identity into the type.
when: Light-mode UI where the darkest text needs to feel intentional and integrated with the palette.
fails: High-contrast accessibility modes, e-ink, or print, where maximum contrast is the requirement.

claim: Set borders and dividers to a light gray, and lighten them further whenever proximity, background fill, or alignment already communicates the grouping.
why: A border is a fallback separator — once spacing does the grouping work, a strong line is redundant and adds visual noise.
when: Cards, table rows, input outlines, and section splits inside an already well-spaced layout.
fails: Layouts with tight spacing or no grouping cues, where the border is the only thing carrying the boundary and must stay visible.

claim: In dark mode, reserve pure white for only the single highest-priority element per view (primary action label, active state) and render all other text in progressively dimmer grays.
why: Full-brightness white on a dark field causes glare and eye strain, so brightness becomes a scarce resource that should be spent on the one thing you want looked at first.
when: Dark themes, especially for reading-heavy or long-session interfaces.
fails: Dimming so far that secondary text fails contrast against the dark surface, or when the theme is used in bright ambient light where reduced values wash out.

claim: Compress the value range more aggressively in dark mode than in light mode — the step from primary to secondary text should be larger, since dark mode starts closer to the glare ceiling.
why: Light mode can safely run text near the dark end, but dark mode's bright end is uncomfortable, so the usable range shifts and the spacing between tiers changes with it.
when: Building a dark theme as a counterpart to an existing light theme.

claim: Do not mirror a light palette into dark mode by simple inversion; re-derive each tier against the dark surface.
why: Inversion maps near-black text onto near-white text, which is exactly the glare case dark mode is meant to avoid.
when: Porting an existing light theme to dark.

claim: Audit a finished screen by counting the elements at absolute #000 or #FFF — if more than one or two per view, redistribute them across gray tiers.
why: Both extremes act as attention magnets; using them everywhere means nothing stands out and the design reads as unrefined.
when: Design review and polish passes before handoff.

claim: Do not generate a dark theme by inverting light-mode colour values; author a separate palette against dark-mode's own constraints.
why: Inversion carries over relationships tuned for a light ground — surface separation, text tint, and accent saturation all behave differently against dark, so the mechanical result is legible but visibly amateurish.
when: Adding a dark theme to an existing light-mode product, or generating one via a token flip or CSS filter.

claim: Increase the lightness gap between adjacent dark surfaces — borders, cards, and page background need a larger numeric step than the equivalent light-mode surfaces to read as separate planes.
why: Perceived contrast compresses at the dark end of the lightness range, so a step size that separates two light greys will look like a single flat colour when inverted into darks.
when: Setting elevation, card, and border tokens for a dark theme.

claim: Set default dark-mode body text to a light grey rather than pure white.
why: Full-white text on a dark ground produces excessive luminance contrast that fatigues the eye; a slightly dimmed grey is more comfortable for sustained reading.
when: Body copy, secondary labels, and general UI text on dark surfaces.
fails: Elements that carry the most importance — wordmark, headline metric — which should be raised to pure white so hierarchy still reads.

claim: Reserve pure white as the top step of the dark-mode text scale and apply it only to the few highest-priority elements.
why: With body text sitting at grey, white becomes the brightest available value and therefore the strongest emphasis signal; spending it everywhere flattens hierarchy.
when: Establishing a dark-mode text colour ramp with two or three brightness tiers.

claim: Check whether your light-mode 'black' and 'white' are actually tinted, because inverting a tinted near-black yields an obviously coloured light value.
why: A dark purple used as light-mode text inverts to a pale purple, which reads as an unintended colour cast rather than neutral text.
when: Auditing an inverted or auto-generated dark palette for unexpected hue in text and surfaces.

claim: Reduce the saturation of brand and accent colours slightly when carrying them into dark mode.
why: A chroma level that reads as balanced against a white ground becomes overbright and vibrating against dark, so the same hue needs to be pulled back.
when: Porting logos, accent fills, and status colours from a light theme into a dark theme.

claim: Treat dark mode as a colour redesign with its own review pass: surfaces, text ramp, and accents each get inspected and corrected independently rather than as one global transform.
why: The demonstrated fixes touch three separate systems, and no single global adjustment would have produced all of them.
when: Reviewing a dark theme before shipping.

claim: Colour destructive actions (delete, remove, permanently discard) red, not with the brand hue, even when the brand hue looks more cohesive.
why: Red is a learned danger signal; a brand-coloured destructive button reads as merely prominent rather than dangerous, so users approve irreversible actions without registering the risk.
when: Any confirmation dialog, menu item, or button that triggers data loss or an irreversible change.
fails: Brands whose primary colour is already red — there, red loses its warning contrast and destructive actions need a different differentiator (heavier weight, a warning icon, an isolated position, or a distinct destructive tint).

claim: Reserve dedicated success (green) and danger (red) slots in every colour palette as functional tokens, defined independently of the brand hues.
why: Semantic states are a system requirement, not a stylistic choice; if the palette only encodes brand colours, designers are forced to express danger with a hue that doesn't mean danger.
when: Defining or auditing a product colour system, especially when the brand palette contains no red or green.

claim: Judge a semantic colour choice by asking whether the meaning survives without the label — if the button would be ambiguous read as colour alone, the colour is wrong.
why: Colour is scanned before text; a treatment that only makes sense once you've read the label has failed at the moment it needed to work.
when: Reviewing any state, action, or status treatment where colour carries meaning.
fails: Colour-blind users and greyscale contexts — colour alone is never sufficient, so pair it with an icon or explicit wording rather than treating hue as the whole signal.

claim: Rank semantic colour conventions by how strictly they're enforced: destructive red is non-negotiable, while notification/badge red is a soft convention you may substitute with a brand colour.
why: Destructive red prevents user harm, so deviation carries real cost; notification red only draws attention, a job any high-contrast accent can do — so it is available for brand expression.
when: Deciding where a brand can express itself within a semantic system and where it must defer.
fails: Notification colour that also carries severity (error counts, alerts, critical warnings) — there it inherits the danger meaning and should stay red.

claim: When brand consistency and semantic clarity conflict on the same element, resolve in favour of the semantic meaning and spend the brand colour on the safe or preferred action instead.
why: Cohesion is an aesthetic gain; a mis-signalled destructive action is a usability failure, and the two are not equal stakes.
when: Dialogs and toolbars where a brand-coloured primary action sits next to a destructive one.

claim: Design semantic colours as light/dark-mode pairs from the outset, not as a single hex value.
why: A red tuned for a light surface loses its urgency or vibrates against a dark one; the signal must hold in both themes to be reliable.
when: Building a palette that ships with a dark mode.

claim: Derive interaction states from the base color by transforming it rather than picking unrelated colors: hover = a lighter/brighter version of the base, active/pressed = a darker version, disabled = a desaturated version.
why: Keeping every state as a mathematical relative of the base color guarantees they read as the same component in different conditions, and makes the state set trivial to generate for any new color you introduce.
when: Defining the state palette for any interactive element — buttons, chips, list rows, icon buttons — in a design system or component library.
fails: When the base color is already grayscale, desaturation cannot signal disabled, so you must fall back to a lightness change instead; and on very dark or very light base colors one direction of the lighten/darken pair may run out of range and need to invert.

claim: Signal a disabled control with a low-contrast fill plus low-contrast label text and no other affordance — no icons, no helper labels, no strikethrough.
why: A control that fails the contrast level users associate with actionable elements reads as inert immediately; extra cues add visual noise to communicate something color already said.
when: Buttons and form controls that are temporarily unavailable, e.g. a submit button before the form is valid.
fails: Disabled state is the one place low contrast is intentional, but if the disabled control still needs to be discoverable or explained, colour alone leaves screen-reader and low-vision users without the signal — pair it with a disabled attribute and, where the reason matters, an adjacent explanation.

claim: Test every state colour in both light and dark themes before shipping it; prefer state transforms that hold up under theme inversion.
why: State colours are derived from a base that itself flips between themes, so a lighten/darken step that reads correctly on a light background can collapse into the surrounding surface on a dark one.
when: Any product that ships both themes or plans to.

claim: On touch targets, drop hover styling entirely and invest the state budget in a pressed style — typically a slightly darker fill applied for the duration of the touch.
why: Touch devices have no persistent pointer, so hover either never fires or sticks after the tap; a press style is the only feedback that actually maps to the input.
when: Mobile web and native app UI, or responsive components rendered on coarse pointers.
fails: Not addressed for hybrid devices with both touch and mouse, where hover should still be supported — gate it on pointer capability rather than screen width.

claim: Add a pressed state even to elements that look flat and unstyled at rest, such as plain list rows or text links in a mobile list.
why: A momentary darkening gives the tap a physical, depressible quality and confirms the tap registered on the intended row, which a rest-state-only element cannot do.
when: Tappable regions on mobile that carry no button chrome.

claim: Budget for at least four colour values per interactive component — rest, hover, pressed, disabled — when planning tokens, instead of a single brand colour.
why: Every interactive element needs its full state set defined up front; discovering the gap at implementation time produces improvised one-off colours that drift from the system.
when: Building colour tokens or a component spec.

claim: Start a palette with exactly one primary hue — take it from the brand if one exists — before adding any other colour.
why: Reduces an open-ended aesthetic decision to a single choice, and guarantees whatever you build from it is internally coherent.
when: Beginning any interface palette, especially without a colour background or an existing design system.
fails: Products that genuinely need multiple independent hue families up front — data-heavy dashboards with categorical series, or multi-brand/white-label systems.

claim: Derive backgrounds and text colours from the primary hue rather than using pure grey — lighten the primary heavily for surfaces, darken it heavily for text.
why: A trace of the brand hue in the neutrals ties the whole surface to the brand and keeps an otherwise flat, grey layout from reading as generic.
when: Choosing page backgrounds, card surfaces, body copy, and heading colours in a single-brand product.
fails: The tint is strong enough to compete with actual UI colour, or when it pushes text/background contrast below accessible thresholds — the hue shift must not cost legibility.

claim: Formalise the light and dark derivations of your primary into a stepped ramp of fixed values, and reference the ramp steps everywhere instead of one-off hex codes.
why: Components, interaction states, chips, and charts all need predictable relative values; a shared ramp is what makes those consistent across a growing product and is the structure mature teams standardise on.
when: The palette is being reused across more than a handful of components, or more than one person is building UI.

claim: Add a new colour only when a specific interface need demands it — an alert bar, a focus ring, a status chip — rather than expanding the palette speculatively.
why: Need-driven colours arrive with a defined job, so the palette stays small and every entry is justified; speculative colours become decoration nobody can interpret.
when: Growing a palette past the primary, particularly as a beginner without system-design experience.
fails: Reactive-only growth in a large product produces near-duplicate one-off colours; past a certain size the ad-hoc additions need consolidating back into the ramp.

claim: Assign meaning to your status colours using the conventional mapping — blue for informational/trustworthy, red for destructive or urgent, yellow for caution, green for success or newness — and never reuse those hues decoratively.
why: Users read these hues as signals before they read the label; using red as a mere accent trains people to ignore your real warnings.
when: Alerts, validation messages, toasts, status chips, destructive buttons, and any state feedback.
fails: The brand primary is itself red or green, so the semantic and brand roles collide and the semantic colours need shifting; also culture-dependent — the red/green mapping is not universal, and red/green pairs alone fail colour-blind users, so pair colour with an icon or text.

claim: Before shipping any colour, be able to state the job it does; if the only answer is 'it looks nice', remove it or replace it with a step from the existing ramp.
why: Colour is a limited signalling channel — every decorative use spends attention that a meaningful use will later need.
when: Reviewing a design or auditing a palette that has grown organically.

claim: Don't port light-mode styles into dark mode unchanged — re-derive border contrast, elevation, and accent intensity for the dark canvas.
why: Perceived contrast is relative to the background; values tuned against white behave very differently against near-black.
when: Building a dark theme from an existing light theme, or maintaining both themes from shared tokens.

claim: Lower the contrast of card and container borders in dark mode — a border that reads as a soft hairline on light backgrounds becomes a harsh outline on dark ones.
why: A light stroke against a dark surface is a high-contrast edge, so it visually shouts louder than the content it's meant to frame.
when: Any bordered surface — cards, panels, inputs, dividers — carried over from a light theme.
fails: Borders that are load-bearing for accessibility, such as focus rings or input outlines, still need to meet non-text contrast minimums and should not be dimmed to the point of disappearing.

claim: Express elevation in dark mode by making the raised surface lighter than the background rather than by casting a drop shadow.
why: Shadows read as darkness, and there is little darkness left to add on an already-dark canvas, so a shadow contributes almost no separation.
when: Any layered UI — cards, modals, sheets, menus, popovers — that relies on shadow for depth in light mode.

claim: Build a stepped ladder of surface values where each level of elevation is one increment lighter than the one beneath it, and keep the page background as the darkest step.
why: If depth is encoded as lightness, a consistent scale is what makes the stacking order legible across the whole product.
when: Defining dark-theme surface tokens for a system with more than one layer of stacking.
fails: Deep nesting eventually runs the lightest surface up toward mid-grey, where it stops reading as dark; cap the number of elevation steps rather than continuing to lighten.

claim: Reduce both the saturation and the brightness of accent fills (chips, badges, tags, alerts) when moving to dark mode.
why: A vivid fill that sat comfortably on white glows and vibrates against a dark field, pulling attention out of proportion to its importance.
when: Any coloured fill reused from the light theme on a dark surface.

claim: For accent components on dark backgrounds, invert the value relationship: use a deep, muted version of the hue as the fill and a light, more saturated version of the same hue as the label.
why: Moving the contrast into the text keeps the component readable while the container stays visually quiet, which preserves the hierarchy between the chip and the content around it.
when: Chips, badges, pills, and status labels that need to be identifiable but not dominant.

claim: Treat the dark base as a hue choice, not a default — deep purple, deep red, or deep green neutrals are all valid alternatives to navy or pure grey.
why: The base hue carries brand character across the largest surface area in the UI, so defaulting to blue-grey discards a cheap source of distinctiveness.
when: Choosing the neutral ramp for a dark theme where brand personality matters.
fails: Pushing chroma too far into the neutrals tints every foreground colour on top of them and can distort brand or semantic colours; keep base saturation low.

claim: Derive dark-mode neutrals as low-saturation tints of a single chosen hue so the whole surface ramp stays coherent rather than mixing greys with tinted panels.
why: A shared hue across all elevation steps makes the lightness ladder read as one material instead of unrelated colours.
when: Constructing a custom-hued dark neutral scale.

claim: When a shadow reads as too heavy, reduce its opacity and increase its blur radius rather than shrinking the offset — soft and faint beats dark and tight.
why: Real diffuse light produces wide, low-contrast falloff; hard dark shadows read as a graphic element rather than as light behaving normally.
when: Correcting default or preset shadows from design tools and CSS libraries, which almost always ship too strong.
fails: Blur pushed far enough with too little opacity leaves a shadow that no longer separates the layer at all — it must still register as separation even if it isn't consciously noticed.

claim: Treat shadows as a light-mode depth tool; do not port the same shadow values into dark mode as your primary elevation cue.
why: Shadows work by darkening a surface, which needs a lighter background to register; on dark surfaces there's little room below to darken into.
when: Building a theme that ships both light and dark modes.

claim: Scale shadow strength to the element's elevation in the stacking order: subtle for cards resting on the page, noticeably stronger for popovers, dropdowns, tooltips and modals that float above other content.
why: Shadow intensity communicates distance from the surface below, so a consistent strength-per-tier scale makes the layer hierarchy readable without labels.
when: Defining an elevation scale in a design system with multiple stacking levels.
fails: Applying popover-strength shadows to inline cards flattens the hierarchy by making everything look like it's floating.

claim: Tune shadow values against the actual foreground and background colours of the surface rather than reusing one global token everywhere.
why: Perceived shadow strength depends on the contrast between the shadow and the surface it falls on, so the same values look right on one background and heavy on another.
when: Placing the same component type on backgrounds of differing lightness or tint.

claim: Build tactile, physically raised controls by pairing an outer drop shadow with an inner shadow — a light inset along the top edge for the lit face and a dark inset along the bottom for the shaded underside.
why: The outer shadow lifts the object off the page while the inset highlight and shade model the object's own volume, together implying a single consistent light source.
when: Designing skeuomorphic or high-affordance buttons, toggles, and pressable controls.
fails: Inner and outer shadows implying different light directions destroys the illusion; also unnecessary on flat design systems where elevation is signalled by colour and border alone.

claim: Use this acceptance test on every shadow: if the shadow is the first thing you notice when you look at the design, dial it back until it isn't.
why: A shadow's job is to communicate depth pre-attentively; once it becomes the focal element it is competing with the content it was meant to support.
when: Final review of any component or screen using elevation.

claim: Never set text directly on a photograph without an intervening contrast layer; treat the overlay as a required component of any image-plus-text composition.
why: Photographic backgrounds vary in luminance across their area, so some glyphs will inevitably land on values too close to the text colour to stay legible.
when: Hero banners, card covers, poster layouts, video thumbnails — anywhere copy sits on top of imagery.
fails: The image region under the text is already a flat, controlled field (studio backdrop, deliberate negative space) with sufficient contrast on its own.

claim: Avoid uniform full-bleed scrims that darken the entire image at one opacity; reserve them for cases where the image is purely decorative texture.
why: A constant tint costs contrast everywhere, including regions with no text, so the photograph loses depth and impact to solve a problem that only exists in one band.
when: The image itself is content the viewer is meant to appreciate — product shots, editorial photography, artwork.
fails: The picture is only atmosphere behind a dense UI, where a flat scrim is the simplest and most predictable route to global legibility.

claim: Default to a linear gradient overlay running from fully transparent at the image end to an opaque-enough colour behind the text block, rather than a flat scrim.
why: It concentrates the contrast cost where the type actually is and leaves the rest of the photograph untouched, satisfying legibility and image fidelity simultaneously.
when: Text is anchored to one edge of the image — bottom captions, top-aligned titles, side-panel copy.
fails: Copy floats in the middle of the frame or is scattered across it; a single-axis gradient has no clean stop to hide and the seam becomes visible.

claim: Ramp the gradient smoothly across a generous distance so the transition into the solid region reads as a fade, not a hard band.
why: An abrupt opacity change registers as a visible edge sitting on top of the photo, which looks like a mistake rather than a designed layer.
when: Any gradient scrim over imagery.

claim: Match the gradient's end colour to the surface the image sits on so the image appears to dissolve into the layout rather than terminate at a rectangle.
why: Converging on the page background makes the overlay read as continuous with the composition instead of as a separate pasted-on shade.
when: Images bleeding into a card, section, or page with a known background colour.
fails: The image floats on a busy or multi-coloured backdrop with no single colour to converge on.

claim: For a more premium finish, stack a progressive blur — blur radius increasing along the same axis as the gradient — on top of the gradient scrim.
why: Blurring destroys the high-frequency detail that competes with letterforms, so the type gains separation from an already-dim area without needing more opacity.
when: Marketing surfaces, hero sections, and mobile app chrome where a contemporary, layered aesthetic is the goal.
fails: Performance-sensitive contexts or low-end devices where stacked blur passes are expensive; also unnecessary when the gradient alone already clears contrast requirements.

claim: Treat progressive blur as an enhancement layered over the gradient, not a replacement for it.
why: Blur alone smears luminance but does not reliably shift it toward or away from the text colour, so contrast can still fail; the gradient does the contrast work and the blur does the aesthetic work.
when: Building a layered overlay stack for image-backed text.

claim: Build a glass surface as a stack of five cheap layers rather than one styled fill: a low-opacity fill, a subtle gradient on top of it, a blur applied to what sits behind, a 1px border, and a soft inner shadow.
why: Each layer simulates a different physical property of glass — translucency, uneven light across the pane, refraction of the background, the cut edge, and light pooling just inside that edge. Any one alone reads as 'flat transparent box'; together they read as a material.
when: Building cards, panels, modals, toolbars, or badges that should sit visually above a dark, textured, or gradient background.
fails: The background behind the surface is flat and uniform — there is nothing for the blur to refract, so the effect costs layers and delivers nothing. Also fails when surfaces stack on surfaces: glass over glass compounds haze until nothing has a clear depth order.

claim: Keep the border at exactly 1px (1 device-independent pixel) and let it be brighter than the fill, not darker.
why: A hairline of light is what separates 'a pane of glass catching a highlight' from 'a rectangle with a stroke'. Any heavier and the border becomes the dominant element instead of the edge condition.
when: Any translucent surface on a dark ground.
fails: On high-DPI screens where a 1px hairline can render sub-pixel and disappear entirely; and at large border radii, where a uniform-brightness border looks wrong compared to one that varies around the curve.

claim: Pair the 1px border with a soft inner shadow so light appears to gather just inside the top edge and fall off toward the centre.
why: Real glass has thickness. The inner shadow is the only cue in the stack that suggests the pane is a solid object with depth rather than a hole cut in the layer above.
when: Whenever you have already added the border — the two are a pair, and the border alone looks thin without it.
fails: On small elements (chips, tags, inputs under ~40px tall) where the inner shadow's falloff has no room and just reads as muddy fill.

claim: Use background blur — blur what is behind the surface — not a blur applied to the surface itself.
why: Blurring the layer blurs its own content and border, destroying the crisp edge that sells the effect. Blurring the backdrop is what makes the panel look like you are seeing through it.
when: Implementing the effect in any tool or CSS context where both operations exist (Figma 'background blur' vs 'layer blur'; CSS `backdrop-filter` vs `filter`).
fails: Never conceptually, but backdrop blur is comparatively expensive to render — avoid it on elements that animate position, on long scrolling lists, or on many simultaneous instances.

claim: Restrict the gradient inside the surface to a narrow value range — a slight lightening across the pane, not a two-colour ramp.
why: The gradient stands in for uneven light falling across glass. Once it becomes a visible colour transition it stops reading as lighting and starts reading as decoration, which cheapens the surface.
when: The gradient layer of the glass stack.
fails: Confusing this with the saturated background gradients the same aesthetic uses. Bold gradients belong behind the glass; the gradient on the glass stays subtle.

claim: Reserve saturated, high-chroma gradients for the background layer and keep the glass surfaces themselves near-neutral.
why: The blur samples colour from behind, so a striking backdrop gradient tints every panel in front of it for free and keeps the whole screen coherent. Colouring both the backdrop and the surface double-tints and turns the panel muddy.
when: Composing a full dark-mode page around this aesthetic.
fails: The backdrop gradient shifts hue dramatically across the page — panels in different regions then read as different components rather than one system.

claim: Give the surface exactly one small motion detail — for example a highlight travelling slowly along the border — and let everything else stay still.
why: One slow, low-contrast animation reads as craft and signals the interface is alive. Animating the fill, the gradient, and the border together reads as a screensaver and undermines the restraint the aesthetic depends on.
when: Hero cards, pricing tiers, feature panels — surfaces the user is meant to notice.
fails: Applied to every card on the page, or to surfaces the user must read or interact with repeatedly, where the movement becomes a distraction. Must also be disabled under reduced-motion preferences.

claim: Calibrate the effect against a 'luxury materials' reference rather than a 'frosted window' one: cool, restrained, expensive-feeling, low contrast between layers.
why: The recipe has a wide range — the same five layers can produce a cheap plastic overlay or a premium panel. The tuning target is what decides which, so name it before you start pushing sliders.
when: Deciding how strong to set opacity, blur radius, border brightness, and shadow spread.
fails: The brand's positioning is playful, retail, or high-energy — this treatment reads as cold and will fight the brand rather than serve it.

claim: Only reach for dark soft glass when the product is trying to signal technical sophistication; treat it as a positioning choice, not a default style.
why: The pattern is currently dense in one category, so it carries specific connotations — infrastructure, AI, developer tooling. Borrowing it puts your product in that conversation whether you intended it or not.
when: Choosing an overall visual direction for a landing page or product surface.
fails: The product is in a category where trust comes from clarity and familiarity — healthcare, government, finance for non-experts — where the aesthetic reads as opaque rather than advanced.

claim: Before shipping a glass surface, verify text contrast against the lightest and darkest points the backdrop can reach behind it, not against a single screenshot.
why: The fill is translucent, so effective text contrast changes with whatever scrolls or animates behind it. A panel that passes over the dark part of a gradient can fail over the bright part.
when: Any translucent surface carrying text, over a non-uniform or scrolling backdrop.

claim: Build palettes from desaturated, tinted colours (baby blue, beige, lavender) rather than restricting yourself to fully saturated hues plus pure black and white.
why: Saturated-or-nothing palettes read as beginner work and leave no room for the subtle steps a real interface needs between its extremes.
when: Choosing any colour scheme, especially when a palette feels harsh, loud, or flat.

claim: Replace #FFFFFF with a slightly off-white in light mode and #000000 with a black tinted toward blue in dark mode.
why: Tinted neutrals soften contrast and tie the surface to the rest of the palette; pure neutrals are the visible signature of an inexperienced designer.
when: Setting background and surface colours for either theme.

claim: Treat AI or generated palettes as a starting point, and pick any additional colour the design needs by eye rather than regenerating the whole palette.
why: Generators produce coherent sets but cannot judge the one extra hue a specific layout demands; that call comes from trained judgement.
when: Extending an existing palette mid-project when the generated set runs short.

claim: Allow exactly one primary call to action per header or comparable section.
why: Two buttons of equal visual weight split the user's attention and neither reads as the intended next step.
when: Any region containing more than one button in close proximity.

claim: When two buttons must coexist, first try removing the second one entirely; only manipulate its styling if it is genuinely a must-have.
why: Deleting the competing action solves the hierarchy problem outright instead of masking it with styling.
when: A section has a secondary button whose necessity has not been challenged.

claim: Style the secondary button as background-free — plain text, an outline, or reduced opacity — so only the primary button carries a filled background.
why: A filled background is the strongest available weight signal; withholding it from the secondary action makes the hierarchy legible without removing the option.
when: Two or more buttons appear side by side and one must be subordinate.

claim: In a destructive confirmation dialog, give the filled background to the destructive action (in red), not to cancel.
why: Primary weight belongs to the action the dialog exists to perform; being dangerous does not demote it, and the red fill carries the warning.
when: Delete, remove, or discard confirmation modals with a confirm/cancel pair.

claim: Do not rely on colour alone to demote a button — drop the fill, or use a border, or lower opacity, and let each of those carry the demotion signal.
why: Several independent weight cues are available, and any one of them is enough to stop the button competing.
when: Deciding how to render a secondary or cancel action.

claim: Judge button hierarchy by proximity: two full-weight buttons far apart in different sections are not a conflict, while the same pair adjacent in a header is.
why: Attention competes locally; buttons only fight when the eye takes them in together.
when: Auditing a layout for competing calls to action.
fails: Applied globally as 'only one filled button per screen', which would strip necessary emphasis from independent sections.

claim: If a gradient or drop shadow isn't clearly improving a composition, delete it outright instead of iterating on its settings.
why: Decorative depth effects are hard to tune well and usually subtract from a design rather than add to it; removal is a faster and more reliable path to a clean result than endless adjustment.
when: You've been nudging shadow or gradient values for a while and the design still feels off.
fails: When the effect is load-bearing — a shadow separating a dropdown, modal, or sticky header from content behind it carries hierarchy information and can't simply be dropped without another separation cue (border, surface tone shift).

claim: Treat gradients as strictly optional: any layout that works with a gradient should also work with a flat fill, so validate it flat before adding one.
why: If the flat version collapses, the gradient was propping up a weak composition rather than decorating a strong one.
when: Deciding whether to introduce a gradient background, button, or overlay.
fails: Gradients used functionally — a scrim behind text over imagery, or a fade masking overflowing content — where the gradient is doing a legibility job, not a decorative one.

claim: Set drop-shadow offsets so the x offset is less than or equal to the y offset, ideally x = 0.
why: Real light comes from above, so shadows fall downward; a horizontal offset larger than the vertical one reads as an unnatural side-lit scene and draws attention to the effect itself.
when: Any UI drop shadow on cards, buttons, modals, or floating panels.
fails: Deliberately stylised or theatrical lighting, or long-shadow illustration styles where the offset is the point.

claim: Set the blur radius to roughly 1.3x–2x the y offset.
why: Blur tied to offset keeps the shadow soft-edged and diffuse in proportion to how far the object floats; too little blur produces a hard duplicate silhouette, too much produces a shapeless haze.
when: Configuring any soft UI shadow.
fails: Very large ambient shadows for big surfaces, where blur often runs well past 2x offset, and hard-edged neo-brutalist shadows that intentionally use zero blur.

claim: Drop the default 25% shadow opacity in your design tool down to roughly 15–20%.
why: Tool presets are calibrated to be visible rather than tasteful; at 25% the shadow reads as a grey smudge instead of implied depth.
when: Immediately after applying a stock shadow preset in Figma or similar.
fails: Dark backgrounds and high-elevation overlays, where a shadow at 15% is invisible and needs more opacity to register.

claim: Scale shadow strength to background darkness — darker surfaces need a stronger, more opaque shadow to be perceptible at all.
why: A shadow works by darkening what's behind it; on an already-dark surface there is less headroom to darken, so the same opacity produces far less contrast.
when: Porting a shadow scale from a light theme to a dark theme, or placing cards on a dark section of a light page.
fails: Dark UIs that convey elevation through lighter surface tints instead of shadows, where piling on shadow opacity does nothing useful.

claim: Derive a whole shadow token from a single y value using the ratios, rather than hand-picking four independent numbers.
why: One input plus fixed ratios makes an elevation scale internally consistent and removes per-instance guesswork.
when: Building a reusable shadow scale or elevation tokens for a design system.

claim: Keep experimenting with shadows and gradients on throwaway work even while deleting them from real work.
why: Judgment about when an effect helps only develops through repeated attempts; the deletion rule is a safety net for shipping, not a ban on practice.
when: Building personal skill versus finishing a client or product design.

claim: Build a hover/selection state animation by duplicating the whole frame per state (option/alt-drag) and changing only the properties that differ, rather than authoring one frame with toggled layers.
why: State-to-state interpolation tools tween matched layers between two frames, so every state needs to exist as its own complete artboard with identical layer structure.
when: Prototyping multi-step UI flows — hover, expand, navigate — in a frame-based design tool.
fails: Long flows with many states become expensive to maintain, since a structural change must be propagated to every duplicated frame; components with variants are the better tool once the state count grows.

claim: To fade an element in or out across animated states, animate the layer's own opacity (the top-level object opacity), not the opacity channel inside its fill.
why: Layer opacity affects the entire object including strokes, effects, and children and is reliably interpolated; fill opacity only affects one paint and can break the tween or leave borders and shadows visible at 0%.
when: Any fade transition on a shape, group, or frame in a design-tool prototype.
fails: When you genuinely want only the fill to change while keeping a stroke fully visible — then fill opacity is the correct control.

claim: Give surfaces a hairline 1px border in a low-contrast neutral instead of relying on fill contrast to separate them from the background.
why: The border does the work of defining edges, which frees the fills to sit in a very narrow value range — the layout still reads as layered even when every surface is near-white.
when: Light, minimal dashboard and productivity UI where you want a calm, flat surface hierarchy.
fails: Dense data-heavy layouts where many adjacent bordered boxes create visual noise; there, spacing or a single elevated surface reads cleaner than outlining everything.

claim: Restrict a light dashboard palette to pure white plus two or three off-whites for surfaces, and carry all separation through borders and typography rather than through varied background tints.
why: A compressed value range keeps the interface feeling clean and lets accent colour and content be the only things that draw attention.
when: Designing the base layer of a light-mode dashboard, sidebar, or panel system.
fails: Interfaces needing strong at-a-glance zone distinction, or any dark-mode adaptation where near-white stacking has no equivalent.

claim: Build drop shadows for pop-up surfaces from a light grey colour rather than semi-transparent black.
why: Transparent black desaturates and muddies whatever sits beneath it; a light grey shadow keeps the underlying whites clean while still producing perceptible lift.
when: Elevation on light backgrounds — menus, tooltips, popovers, cards floating above a white or near-white canvas.
fails: Dark backgrounds or surfaces over photographic/coloured content, where a grey shadow reads as a light halo instead of a shadow.

claim: Treat icon selection and consistency as the primary quality lever in a sidebar, since the rest of the component is only text and dividers.
why: With so few visual elements, icons carry almost all the personality and polish; mismatched stroke weights or styles are immediately obvious.
when: Designing navigation rails, sidebars, and any icon-plus-label list.

claim: Position the hover highlight as a rectangle sitting behind the nav item's text and icon, sized to the row rather than the label.
why: A background shape gives a consistent hit area and hover target across items of differing label lengths, and it can fade independently of the content it highlights.
when: Any list-style navigation with hover or active states.

claim: Decompose a UI animation into its independently-moving parts before building, and construct each part in isolation.
why: Naming the moving pieces up front tells you which layers must be matched across frames, which is what makes the interpolation predictable.
when: Planning any multi-element interface animation.

claim: Ship a style guide alongside the design file so the token values — colours, shadow settings, type — are reconstructable rather than buried in individual layers.
why: Explicit tokens let someone rebuild or extend the design without eyedroppering values off a screenshot.
when: Publishing design files intended for reuse, handoff, or teaching.

claim: Ship both a light and a dark palette and bind them to the OS appearance setting rather than forcing one appearance.
why: The appearance toggle is a first-class system preference on every Mac; an app that ignores it feels foreign to the platform and overrides a choice the user deliberately made.
when: Any macOS (or broadly, any OS-themed) app or interface that defines its own colours.

claim: Do not generate a dark palette by algorithmically inverting the light palette (or vice versa) — author each mode's colours separately.
why: Inversion is a mathematical operation on colour values, but perceived contrast is not symmetric between a bright and a dim viewing context, so the same numeric relationships read differently in each mode.
when: Deriving a second colour mode from an existing one.
fails: As a rough first pass it is acceptable — inversion gets you in the neighbourhood and is a reasonable starting point to then hand-tune, just not a finished result.

claim: In dark mode, push the steps between adjacent surface, border, and text colours further apart than the equivalent steps in light mode.
why: There is less overall light in the interface to differentiate elements, so small colour deltas that separate cleanly on a white background collapse into mush on a dark one.
when: Assigning colours to layered UI — cards on backgrounds, dividers, secondary text, disabled states — in a dark theme.

claim: In light mode, compress the palette — keep the values closer together — instead of driving every pair to maximum separation.
why: A bright background already supplies plenty of luminance separation; adding more on top produces a harsh, unpolished result, whereas a tighter range reads as refined.
when: Building the light theme, especially if its values were carried over from a dark theme.
