fails: Compressing so far that text or interactive elements drop below accessible contrast thresholds — refinement cannot come at the cost of legibility.

claim: Keep hue and colour role identical across modes and vary only the contrast spread, so that the same element is recognisably the same element in either appearance.
why: The two modes should feel different in atmosphere but consistent in identity; if roles or hues shift between them the app reads as two different products.
when: Maintaining a two-mode design system with named colour tokens.

claim: Treat a visually restrained layout as licence to be more adventurous with colour.
why: When structure, spacing, and ornamentation are quiet, colour is the only variable carrying expressive load, so it can take risks without the composition becoming noisy.
when: Simple, sparse app interfaces with few competing visual elements.
fails: Dense or information-heavy layouts, where expressive colour compounds existing visual load.

claim: Work in HSB (hue, saturation, brightness) when generating related colours, not hex; hex is fine for storing and handing off a final value but gives you no axis to move along.
why: HSB separates the three properties you actually want to control, so a colour variation becomes a numeric step on one axis instead of guesswork across six digits.
when: Deriving multiple related tones from a chosen colour inside any design tool with a mode-switchable colour picker.
fails: Handing colours to engineers or design tokens, where hex/RGB is the expected format; also HSB brightness is not perceptual lightness, so it won't guarantee contrast ratios.

claim: Start from exactly one base colour and derive every other colour in the object from it, rather than picking each colour independently.
why: A single origin guarantees the tones belong to the same family, which is what makes a palette read as intentional instead of assembled.
when: Colouring a single illustrated object or component that has multiple surfaces (front, back, band, shadow).
fails: Palettes that need genuine contrast between semantic roles — accent versus neutral, success versus danger — where one hue family is insufficient.

claim: If you have no base colour instinct, pull one from a palette generator (Coolors or similar) instead of stalling on the first decision.
why: The derivation method does the heavy lifting; the base only needs to be defensible, not inspired.
when: Starting a palette with no brand colour or existing constraint.
fails: Brand, accessibility, or client constraints already dictate the base colour.

claim: To generate the next darker tone in a family, hold hue constant and apply a fixed step: saturation +20, brightness -10. Apply the same step again from that result to get a third tone.
why: A constant step keeps the perceptual gap between tones even, and raising saturation as brightness drops prevents dark tones from going muddy and grey.
when: Building a 3-tone set of front / mid / deep surfaces on one object or component.
fails: Once saturation hits 100 or brightness bottoms out, further steps stop producing visible change — the ratio needs rescaling for very light or very saturated bases.

claim: Layer a hue shift on top of the saturation/brightness step: rotate hue about 20 points toward blue for each successively darker tone.
why: Hues carry inherent perceived lightness, so nudging darker tones toward the intrinsically darker part of the wheel makes the depth read as light behaviour rather than as a flat brightness slider drop.
when: Refining a derived palette that already looks correct but flat; used for shadow and receding surfaces.
fails: Rotating too far turns a tint into a visibly different colour and breaks the family reading; the direction also inverts if you are generating lighter tones instead of darker ones.

claim: Treat blues and purples as the perceptually darkest hues and yellows and reds as the lightest, and use that ordering to decide which way to rotate hue when you want a tone to read darker or lighter.
why: Perceived lightness varies by hue independently of the brightness value, so hue rotation is a second lever on depth.
when: Any decision about which direction to shift hue for shadows, highlights, or depth in flat illustration and UI surfaces.

claim: Produce both the hue-shifted and non-hue-shifted versions and compare them side by side before committing.
why: The refinement is a matter of taste rather than correctness, and the difference is only legible in direct comparison.
when: Choosing between two defensible palette treatments.

claim: Encode the palette rule as a repeatable numeric increment you can reapply, not as a one-off eyeballed colour.
why: A stated increment scales to any number of tones and stays consistent across a project, which eyeballing does not.
when: Any project needing more than two related tones, or consistency across multiple assets.

claim: Never ship #FFFFFF or #000000 as a page background; instead take your accent hue and push it to a very dark (dark mode) or very light (light mode) value, and use that as the canvas.
why: A tinted canvas carries the brand hue into every pixel of the screen rather than confining colour to buttons and links, so the whole interface feels intentional and unified instead of like default browser chrome.
when: Setting the base surface colour of any screen, in either light or dark mode, when you already have an accent colour.
fails: Not addressed in the chapter — though the tint must stay subtle enough to read as neutral; pushing saturation too high turns a background into a coloured block that competes with content.

claim: For a light theme, pair a 50-value background with the 500-value of the same hue as the accent.
why: Both swatches come from the same hue ramp, so they are guaranteed to be harmonious, and the tonal gap between 50 and 500 gives enough contrast for accent elements to read clearly against the canvas.
when: Building a light-mode interface fast, or when you don't trust your own colour mixing.
fails: A 500 accent on a 50 background may not clear text-contrast thresholds for small body copy — it is sized for buttons, icons and fills, not fine type.

claim: For a dark theme, pair a 950-value background with the 300-value of the same hue as the accent.
why: The accent must be lighter than the canvas in dark mode, so the ramp inverts: a near-black tinted base with a light, desaturated-feeling accent that stays legible without glowing.
when: Building a dark-mode interface and needing a background/accent pair that works immediately.
fails: Not addressed.

claim: Pull both background and accent from the same numbered step of a single systematic colour ramp rather than eyeballing two independent hex values.
why: A ramp already encodes consistent lightness and chroma relationships between steps, so any pair drawn from it inherits that consistency — the failure mode of hand-picked colours is that the relationship is accidental.
when: Any project without a bespoke design system or a dedicated colour designer.
fails: When brand colours are fixed and don't map cleanly onto a generic ramp, you have to generate a custom ramp from the brand hue instead of borrowing one.

claim: Validate a colour decision by pointing at shipped products that already use it, not by reasoning about it in the abstract.
why: Widely used software that a designer trusts is evidence the treatment survives real content, real contrast requirements and real users — it de-risks a choice that might otherwise feel too unusual to ship.
when: Deciding whether an unconventional-feeling treatment is safe to adopt.
fails: The cited product may have constraints or brand equity you don't, so precedent justifies the technique but not a literal colour copy.

claim: In dark mode, express elevation with stepped surface background colours rather than drop shadows; each layer that sits 'above' another gets its own lighter surface value.
why: A shadow is a dark smudge on an already-dark ground, so it produces almost no contrast and reads as nothing; a lighter surface is the only cheap signal the eye can pick up.
when: Dark themes, or any interface whose base canvas is dark enough that black shadows have no contrast against it.
fails: Light themes, where shadows still work and colour-stepped surfaces alone can look flat or muddy; also breaks if step counts push surfaces so light that they stop reading as dark mode.

claim: Generate each elevation step in HSB by adding roughly 4-6 to brightness and subtracting roughly 10-20 from saturation, keeping hue fixed.
why: Holding hue constant keeps the palette coherent while the brightness bump does the elevation work; cutting saturation prevents the lighter surfaces from turning into a vivid, saturated colour as they climb.
when: Building a dark-mode surface ramp from a single tinted base colour (e.g. a dark blue background) in any HSB-capable tool.
fails: Very desaturated or pure-neutral bases, where saturation has no room to drop; and highly saturated brand hues, where a fixed numeric step may not hold perceived contrast.

claim: Apply the same brightness/saturation step repeatedly to build a multi-level surface ramp for dense layouts, rather than inventing a fresh colour per layer.
why: A consistent per-step delta makes the layering system predictable and self-consistent, so a viewer can infer depth ordering from surface lightness alone.
when: Layout with several nested containment levels — dashboards, panels inside panels, cards inside sections, modals over cards.
fails: Deep stacks eventually run out of usable range; past a handful of steps the surfaces converge on light grey and stop reading as a dark theme.

claim: Treat the card as the unit of depth in dark mode: wrap each content group in a container with its own surface value instead of relying on spacing or borders alone.
why: If elevation is carried by fill colour, there must be a filled region to carry it; grouping content into cards gives the colour step something to attach to.
when: Grouping related content on a dark canvas where you want the group to read as separate from what surrounds it.

claim: Define dark-mode surfaces as a small ordered token set (base, level 1, level 2, ...) derived by a fixed HSB rule, and assign components to levels rather than picking colours ad hoc.
why: A rule-generated ramp keeps every screen's layering consistent and makes the system extensible when a new nesting level appears.
when: Any dark theme that will be used across more than one screen or by more than one person.

claim: Create depth with foreground/background offsets instead of relying only on shadows.
why: A visible positional separation makes an element read as a layer above its background and can feel more intentional than added shadow alone.
when: Buttons, cards, image blocks, or framed elements need stronger hierarchy or tactile separation.

claim: Turn an offset layer into a hover state by duplicating the component, shifting its background layer, and linking the states in the prototype.
why: The small positional change makes the layered construction legible and adds an immediate interactive response.
when: A UI element supports hover input and needs lightweight feedback.
fails: Touch-only contexts where hover is unavailable.

claim: Separate page regions with deliberately different backgrounds to create depth between sections.
why: A background change establishes distinct visual planes and prevents adjacent content areas from blending together.
when: Long pages contain multiple content groups that need structural separation.

claim: In dark interfaces, place lighter card surfaces over a darker page background to make cards appear closer to the viewer.
why: Value contrast between the page plane and card plane creates a foreground-versus-recessed-background relationship.
when: Designing dark-mode cards, panels, or grouped content.

claim: Treat dark mode as a separate palette: switch text to a light value and retune accent colours instead of only changing the page background to dark.
why: Colours that work on light backgrounds can become visually aggressive or poorly balanced on dark ones.
when: Adapting a modern website or app from a light interface to dark mode.
fails: The brand palette, accessibility requirements, or content type calls for a different theme strategy.

claim: Reduce the perceived harshness of saturated accents in dark mode by shifting them to a lighter, less visually heavy variant while preserving their hue family.
why: Highly saturated accents can overpower a dark interface; a lighter blue integrates more naturally.
when: A bright primary or accent colour feels too intense after a dark-mode conversion.
fails: The adjusted colour no longer meets required contrast or brand constraints.

claim: Use translucent frosted-glass surfaces on cards and decorative colour fields to add depth and polish to a dark modern UI.
why: Layered translucent surfaces prevent the dark palette from feeling flat and make the composition feel more intentional.
when: The design has card-based content and a decorative background that can support layered visual treatment.
fails: Readability, performance, or a restrained product style makes blur and translucency inappropriate.

claim: When a layout feels sterile but does not need structural redesign, replace selected pure-white backgrounds with a coordinated range of off-white tones.
why: Small shifts in background colour add warmth and visual grouping while preserving the existing layout and content.
when: A mostly white interface feels flat, generic, or visually disconnected.
fails: The added surface colours reduce text contrast, blur hierarchy, or conflict with the product’s established colour system.

claim: Use a subtle textured or image-based background with a low-key noise overlay when a large surface needs more character without competing with content.
why: Restrained texture prevents an empty background from feeling lifeless while keeping the foreground readable.
when: A spacious landing page or section has enough open area for ambient visual treatment.
fails: Texture becomes prominent enough to distract from copy, controls, or readability.

claim: Keep default values visually restrained and reserve stronger fill or colour for meaningful state differences.
why: Equally prominent defaults compete with the changes users need to notice.
when: Settings chips and selection controls.
fails: Restrained defaults still need readable contrast and recognizable affordances.

claim: Reduce competing emphasis around an important value before making that value more saturated or bold.
why: Prominence depends on contrast with neighbouring elements.
when: Multiple chips or controls compete for attention.
fails: A critical alert can still need explicit emphasis when surrounding content cannot be subdued.
